In the Vegreville riding we have a park known as Elk Island park, which is so beautiful that if I tried to describe it adequately, words would wholly fail me. Therefore I do not wish to spoil the picture by any word description of my own, but I suggest to the minister that when he finally decides to issue circulars, or whatever he wishes to do in regard to this matter, he let the tourists who visit that part of the country know that a few miles south of Lamont there is a park called Elk Island park. In this circular I hope he will picture this park in larger capital letters than any other parks that have been mentioned here to-day.

So far as tourists are concerned, may I say there is nothing finer or more attractive in Canada than the Prince Albert National park. There are other parts of Prince Albert constituency which are

equally beautiful, and I hope the tourist bureau will do justice to them, or rather attempt so to do.

Hon. members have all been singing the praises of their respective constituencies. In the constituency of Lisgar we have a resort that is recognized by both political parties as the finest in Manitoba or, indeed, in the west. In 1925, when Right Hon. Arthur Meighen was aspiring to become prime minister and was touring t'he country, his party chose Rock lake as a place to give a great demonstration, and it was truly a magnificent crowd that assembled there to hear the right hon. gentleman. Similarly when my right hon. leader (Mr. Mackenzie King) toured Manitoba and the west a short time ago, the Liberal party chose Rock lake as the most suitable place for the clans to come together to welcome their chief. So we have the endorsation of both political parties that Rock lake is the finest spot in Manitoba.
I think it would be very desirable that a Small portion of this appropriation or some other money should be spent on building just a few miles of highway to make a better connection between that beautiful summer resort and the country to the south. That would attract large numbers of tourists from the south. As I have said, we have the endorsation of both political parties that Rock lake is the one point at which they can best show their appreciation of their respective leaders.

I am surprised, as I listen to all the boasting about the beauties of the maritime provinces and western Canada, that everybody seems to have forgotten that when one goes down to the maritimes, one must go through the beautiful province of Quebec. The loveliness of the south shore of the St. Lawrence, especially between Quebec and the maritime provinces, is unequalled in -Canada. I appeal to the Minister of Railways, who travelled last year through this famous gardqn that we call the Gaspe peninsula, and I ask hon. members when going down to the maritime provinces to stop on the way at Rimouski, where they will be well received.

There is one practical suggestion I should like to make to the minister which has not so far been offered. The minister in his opening address I think said that when the bureau was sending out pictures and advertising matter, the pictures would be sent out without the provinces being specifically mentioned on them. For instance, if pictures of mountains or lakes are used, those pictures would not inform the public where the particular spots are. Speaking from a little experience I know the people of the United

Supply-Railways-Tourists
States are not as discerning as we are in this country. A car may enter the republic from any province and the people there will simply say: "Oh, there is a Canadian car," irrespective of what province it may come from. I do not know whether we are better educated in this country, but I know that when American cars come here we observe what state they come from. I would thereforce suggest to the minister that in the pictures and photographs that go out it would be well that the provinces in which the places shown are situated should be mentioned, so that tourists may know where to find that beautiful scenery. I shall not take any more time talking about British Columbia, but if material for the proposed advertising is to be culled from Hansard I would just say that if any visitor comes to Canada and fails to see British Columbia his visit has been in vain.

So much has been said about the beauties of the various provinces that I do not wish to add anything on that aspect of the matter, because other members know a good deal more about it than I do. Yet there are many beautiful parts in Manitoba, and not the least of our beauties is the Red river, and the Red river flows through North Winnipeg. But it is not now the beauty spot it once was; in fact the Red river to-day in the neighbourhood of Winnipeg has become more or less a plague spot that people try to get away from. So I have a suggestion to make to the government which I hope they will not only take into serious consideration but on which they will act in the very near future. The Red river has been polluted with sewage both in the United States and in Canada. At the present time Winnipeg and neighbouring municipalities have made a request to the government for assistance in providing sewage disposal works. I raise the question because I should like to be able to say for the Red river what others have been saying for their various constituencies. I should like the tourist bureau in getting out literature concerning Winnipeg and the adjoining districts to be able to show the Red river as one of its beauty spots, but before that can be, something must be done in regard to scientific and up to date sewage disposal. I suggest to the acting Prime Minister, who is now discussing the matter with the Minister of Railways, that prompt action be taken by the federal government in the way of assistance to the province of Manitoba to restore the attractions of the Red river.

I do not want to take up much of the time of the committee, but I have listened to everyone praising his own
province and merely want to say that there is no need of singing the praises of New Brunswick; its beauties are too well known. I merely call the attention of the committee to two things which we possess in New Brunswick which are not found elsewhere, namely the reversing falls at Saint John and the heavy rush of water in the Petitcodiac river creating wihat is known as the Moncton bore. That is all I want to say.

Before this vote carries I should like to say a word on behalf of the eastern townships of the province of Quebec. I do not need to say much, but I would draw attention to the fact that it is one of the finest scenic areas in the whole dominion and has natural attractions unsurpassed anywhere. It is a region of rivers, lakes and mountains galore. I know of one mountain 2,900 feet high from which I can view twenty-one small lakes, all teeming with fish, mostly trout. Of course they are not as large as they catch in some parts of the lower provinces or in British Columbia, but that does not seem to make much difference to the ordinary fisherman. As a general rule the ordinary fisherman is as much interested in what he takes with him and his surroundings when fishing as in what he catches, and I may say that remark is not confined to liquid refreshments.
It seems that this appropriation is about half what it should be, if all the requisitions of hon. members who have spoken are to be met.
I just want to remind the committee that I have the privilege of representing the Garden of Eden in the county of Pictou.
What about Eve?

She is there too and we
also still use the original language of the garden of Eden. So we have a history of at least six thousand years of close association with the early times of the race. No one could find a better place ini all Canada in which to spend a summer holiday, particularly in view of the reductions in excise and the reduction of customs duty on West India rum of which we have heard this afternoon.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. J. MANION (Minister of Railways and Canals):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on the last occasion this bill was before the house I had only three or four minutes before nine o'clock in which to speak. In that time I pointed out some circumstances which, so as to make my argument more complete, I shall repeat to-night.
In the first place I indicated that a bill such as the one before us is really not a private bill, from the standpoint of the functions of parliament, because parliament is not a rate making body. This is not the body which sets railway freight or passenger rates. Neither the government nor the parliament o(f Canada has the proper machinery with
[Mr. Turnbull.l
which to deal with this very complicated matter. The matter of freight rates is perhaps one of the most complicated which could be placed before any commission, and one which requires special machinery !by way of experts and authorities.
I pointed out, further, that if freight rates were set in this House of Commons we would have so many bills like the present one placed before the House of Commons that we would have no time for anything else. The matter of freight rates would become a political question because almost every constituency in Canada has some particular commodity in which it is interested, and each member would be subjected to public pressure to bring before the House of Commons questions of freight rates on the commodities produced in his particular section of the country. As a result there would be the danger of log rolling, in the worst sense of the term. We would have one member assisting another in his effort to secure satisfactory freight rates on the understanding that, in return, the other would assist the first. Ultimately parliament would be inundated with bills to cut down freight rates on pulpwood, wheat, hay, potatoes or some other commodity. Speaking of potatoes may I say that only within the last week I have had communications from people outside the house and have had a number of hon. members approach me regarding the rate on potatoes from one section of the country to another. Special rates for potatoes have been requested by the maritime provinces and by the province of Quebec. Therefore I submit that we would have an impossible situation if the parliament of Canada were permitted to deal with freight rates.
The hon. member now sponsoring the bill has introduced a similar bill on four previous occasions and, incidentally, has approached the board of railway commissioners in regard to the same matter. Receiving a judgment from the board which was not in his favour, he has appealed to the privy council. That appeal, by the way, is still before the privy council and will have to be dealt with in the future.
In his speech the other evening he made a number of statements upon only a few of which I shall now touch. I pointed out on the previous occasion that the export rates are set for the purpose of permdtitng the products affected to compete in the world market. Generally speaking they are not set on the basis adopted in connection with domestic rates, because domestic rates are enforced so as to deal with the matter from the stand-

Railway Act-Rates on Grain
point of local consumption. When a commodity comes under an export rate it is on the way to a foreign market and is in a position where it must compete with the products of different countries of the world. Therefore, generally speaking export rates in Canada are not on the same basis as domestic rates, nor are they on the same basis even so far as mileage is concerned. For example-I assume my hon. friend knows this but the house generally may not-the rates from Edmonton to Vancouver, Calgary to Vancouver, and Edmonton to Prince Rupert are all exactly the same, 20 cents per 100 pounds, yet the distance from Edmonton to Vancouver is 765 miles, from Calgary to Vancouver 642 miles, and from Edmonton to Prince Rupert 973 miles.
Those are export rates?

Yes, and they are all put
on the same basis because if one or the other route had an advantage even according to mileage it would get all the grain exported-* I am speaking of grain at the moment-and the others would get none. It is the same with regard to Halifax and St. John. The rates from Montreal to Halifax and St. John are exactly the same, for the reasons I have Just mentioned, although there is a great difference in the mileage.
The United States export rates are much higher than ours. It is true that in some cases, perhaps many cases, their domestic rates are lower than our normal domestic rate, but their export rate, which is also their domestic rate, is considerably higher than our export rate. For the information of the house I am going to put on Hansard a few of those rates, though some of these rates have been put on Hansard before.
The rate from Shelby, Montana, to Seattle, domestic or export, a distance of 757 miles, is 38i cents per 100 pounds. The rate from Bissell, Alberta, to Vancouver, a distance of 758 miles, just one mile more, is 20 cents; that is the Canadian rate is 20 cents as against the American rate of 38J cents. From Livingston, Montana, to Seattle, a distance of 897 miles, the rate is 39 cents, while from Greenshields, Alberta, to Vancouver, a distance of 893 miles, practically the same mileage, the rate is 22 cents; that is 22 cents on the Canadian side as against 39 cents on the American side. I am informed by railway authorities that practically all the rates on grains for export are in favour of Canada; that is they are lower to the Canadian shipper. It is true that the domestic rates in the United States, which are the same as the export rates, are lower in some
cases than ours, but due to the special domestic rate which through efforts of my own to a large extent and of the Minister of Agriculture we obtained about a year and a half ago from the prairie provinces to British Columbia, our feed grain rates are lower than the rates on the same quality of grain for domestic consumption in the United States. The same is true of our emergency rates obtained a few months ago for the purpose of shipping to the United States grains of lower quality, what are called feed grains. So on those two grades of grain, feed grains and grains of the lower grade-I have forgotten the exact classification-our rates are considerably lower than United States rates.
My hon. friend complained, and rightly, that our rate on burnt wheat unfit for human consumption was as high as the rate on other grains, but recently the railway commission instructed the railways that burnt wheat should be treated on the same basis as the lower grades of wheat moving from the prairie provinces to British Columbia.
My hon. friend also mentioned the rates from Calgary or Edmonton, or from the prairies for that matter, to Vancouver, as compared with the rates to Fort William. The rate from Calgary to Vancouver is 20 cents, and the rate from Calgary to Fort William is 26 cents. But the hon. gentleman, if I understood him aright, in comparing these two rates brought into the comparison the distances. I must submit to him and the house that grain at the head of the lakes is not in the same position as grain at Vancouver because grain at Vancouver is all the year round right on the seaboard, and in a position to be shipped across to Europe, whereas at Fort William it has to go at least one thousand miles to Montreal, and a great deal further if it is shipped in winter to Halifax or Saint John. So there is no fairness in comparing the rate on grain from the prairies to Fort William with the rate from the prairies to Vancouver, because the grain at Fort William is still inland and has to go at least as far as Montreal, and in winter to Halifax or Saint John, before it is in a position to be shipped to Europe.
But Vancouver has this other advantage. It is open the year round, whereas it is possible to ship grain from the head of the lakes by water only during seven months of the year, and as the rate is so high by rail from Fort William to Montreal or to the maritimes, that is practically a paper rate; in other words, almost no grain is shipped from the head of the lakes to either Montreal or the maritime
Railway Act-Rates on Grain

ports of Halifax and Saint John in the winter, and it is only during seven months of the year it can be exported. Therefore when grain gets into the elevators at the head of the lakes it stays there till the following spring because the rate is too high to ship it out.
It is true that the domestic rate from the head of the lakes to Montreal is lower than the export rate, but they are both paper rates. Neither of them is used because grain can go from the head of the lakes in the summer by water to Montreal for something under 4 cents a bushel; in fact, the rate during the whole season of 1933 averaged 3-79 cents a bushel. It is obvious therefore that when grain can be shipped in the summer for 3'79 cents a bushel, less than 4 cents a bushel, by water, it will not go by rail and pay a rate of 25 or 34 cents per 100 pounds, as the case may be, from the head of the lakes to Montreal or the maritime ports. Water competition controls, and my hon. friend complained a little of that, I think; but the fact remains that if the railways are to get any of the traffic between any two points they must compete with whatever other competition there is, and I have given the rate for the water competition. That competition is so severe that except for an emergency small shipment, a carload or some very small shipment, the railways will not get any, and even then they would have to compete to a certain extent with the lake rate or the lake and rail rate.
Another point which I wish to submit to the house is that the railways are to-day giving to Canada, as I stated and as has been stated by many railway authorities-I am not one of them-the lowest rates in the world for like distances, and consequently in view of the financial condition not only of the Canadian National but of the Canadian Pacific it would be of the most serious consequence to them if they were forced to give rates which would not pay them. Remember that if the railways of Canada, which are to-day having great difficulty in getting along at all, were forced to cut down their rates still further, they might be put in the position of threatening very seriously the maintenance of adequate railway services from one part of Canada to the other. AH railways, not only Canadian railways but the railways on the American side, have, during the past few years, found it necessary to defer maintenance on their roads because they have not been earning sufficient money to provide themselves with rails and railway equipment, even with ties and various other materials which they require to keep them going so far as maintenance is concerned.

Therefore if they were forced to lower their rates still further they would to a still greater degree be forced to defer maintenance; that would automatically lead to a greater amount of unemployment among those who carry on the maintenance, and that would mean a greater tax upon the Canadian people.
It is also well to remember that this country because of its great distances cannot get along without railway services, and if we put the railways into still greater difficulties we are really cutting our own throats because we are putting ourselves in a position in which we could not continue to exist.
It is perhaps as well to point out that the Canadian Pacific Railway in 1934, so far as my information goes, just earned its interest on its bonds, and the Canadian National, as this house knows well, is about fifty million dollars, in round figures, short of earning its interest payments for the past year. I submit that they could not stand very much pressure in the way of lower freight rates although individual sections might be served.
The hon. member also argued that the rates to British Columbia should be lower on certain lines through the rockies because of their lower grades. He did not mention an obvious fact, that the construction costs through the mountains are exceedingly heavy and the running of trains is difficult and sometimes hazardous. There is hardly any local business through the mountains. We all remember that only a few weeks ago a severe snow storm tied up trains in the Rocky mountains for as long as nine or ten days. This is something which does not occur in any other section of the country and it illustrates the difficulty of operating trains through the mountains.
I do not know that my hon. friend used the argument the other evening, but it has been argued before that the parliament of Canada passed the Crowsnest pass rates. However, it should be remembered that the act covering these rates was passed in 1897, seven years before the board of railway commissioners was set up. At that time parliament was justified in acting, but at the present time I submit that it is not justified in dealing with such a complicated question as this. I might tell the house that the board of railway commissioners has been rarely overruled by the government. I made it my business today to obtain some information from the board as to the number of appeals which have been made against their judgments They furnished me with the information that appeals to the governor in council had been made from forty-five of their judgments in

Railway Act-Rates on Grain
the period from February 1, 1904, when they were organized, to December 31, 1934. Of those appeals, forty-two were disallowed, referred back, dismissed or abandoned; in other words, the judgments were not interfered with. Of the three appeals which were allowed, one was in connection with a railway crossing, nothing whatever to do with freight rates. Another was in connection with the National Dairy Council of Canada and was against a ruling of the board dated November 21, 1922, in connection with a twenty per cent increase in cream rates. This was a protest against an increase in rates. The third appeal was made in 1924 when the governments of Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba appealed from order number 408 dated October 14, 1924, regarding the Crows-nest pass rates. This appeal was allowed because of a decision of the supreme court. The supreme court had decided the case and the government merely accepted its decisions. In the period from 1904 until the end of 1934 there were forty-five appeals and in no case was a decision given by the government putting into effect a lower freight rate so far as any normal or standing freight rate was concerned.
I shall not take up any more time except to say just a few more words. I compliment the hon. gentleman upon his persistence. He has had this matter up before this house four times; he has had it up before the board of railway commissioners, and he is now making an appeal. However I submit with all deference that his persistence does not make his bill a proper one. I do admit that the freight rate structure of Canada is antiquated. It is in a more or less chaotic condition and I believe there will have to be something in the way of a complete investigation into the freight rates in the near future with the purpose of wiping out some of the chaos which exists and putting the freight rates in a more equitable condition. While I admit that an investigation is needed, that is a different question from the parliament of Canada attempting to adjudicate upon a question of this kind. The government feels, as we have felt for the last four years, that we cannot take the position of making freight rates in this house and we must therefore oppose the second reading of this bill. I submit to hon. members opposite with the best intention in the world that if they are by any chance the winners at the next election and the hon. member introduces a similar bill, they are likely to be embarrassed due to the fact that some of them have voted as they have. The government
of that day might be in the rather awkward position, if it were consistent, of trying to adjudicate upon a question of this kind. I merely mention this in passing.
It is a long way off.

Yes, I think probably it is, but I am just pointing that out. For these reasons I submit that this question is not one upon which this parliament could give a decision favourable to the hon. gentleman.

[DOT] Mr. Speaker, I intend to detain the house but a few moments in connection with the bill introduced by the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid). This bill seeks to add to subsection 5 of section 325 of the Railway Act the following words:
-and to all such traffic moving westwardly from Fort William, and from all points on all lines of railway west of Fort William, to Vancouver, British Columbia and to points on the Pacific coast,-
I desire to take this opportunity of complimenting the hon. member for having made his plea year after year ever since he came to this house. He has made this matter a live issue as far as the interests of the people of British Columbia are concerned. Regardless of any political affiliations he has acted in their interests and the interests of the people of western Canada generally.
In the few minutes I have at my disposal I shall refer to the five reasons given by the Minister of Railways (Mr. Manion) for opposing this measure. Those five reasons, while they may be worthy in themselves, are entirely inconsistent in the general composite structure of the opposition which he is offering. The first submission made by the minister was that parliament is not the proper body to make freight rates, that the building up of a freight rate structure should be left to a body of technical experts. He contended that the board of railway commissioners had been specifically created for this purpose. I agree with the minister so far as the general details of a freight rate structure are concerned, but here we have at stake a basic principle of fundamental justice. When we must make a decision in regard to such a principle, the proper body to adjudicate upon the equity and justice of this principle is the court of last resort, the parliament of the Dominion of Canada, and not any body of experts. I am endeavouring to differentiate between the details of a common freight rate structure as they apply to any section of the country and
Railway Act-Rates on Grain

a violation of the basic principle of fundamental justice and rankest discrimination against a splendid section of this country.
The second point made by my hon. friend had nothing whatever to do with the ability or inability of this parliament to adjudicate a question of justice which concerns British Columbia and western Canada. I cannot quote him word for word but the sense of his remarks was that there was no fairness in comparing rates from the prairies to Vancouver with those from the prairies to Fort William. He stated that many of the rates applying in eastern Canada were paper rates, in other words, that British Columbia and in particular the ports of Vancouver and Prince Rupert, must suffer the inequalities and injustices of an unfair structure of freight rates because the ports are open the year round. We are being made to pay for our climatic superiority through an unjust discrimination in favour of certain sections of eastern Canada.
I have come now to the third reason given by the minister. He said that if the railways are going-

I am sorry to interrupt
my hon. friend, but I am sure he wishes to be fair. I was dealing not with the rates from the prairies to Fort William but with those from the head of the lakes to Montreal. I say this so that the record may be straight. That was a different thing from the rate from the prairies to Fort William.
How long has this injustice been going on?
It has been going on -
It went on for ten years under the previous government.

I am not discussing what has happened under either party; I am arguing for simple justice for the west. With all respect to the minister, I took down his words and I think Hansard will bear me out when I quote him as having said that there is no fairness in comparing the rates from the prairies to Vancouver with the rates from the prairies to Fort William.
That is correct.
And he said that the rates from the head of the lakes to Montreal were largely paper rates and were dictated by cheaper water competition.
My hon. friend has me right now; he did not have me right the other time.

I am
dealing with two different things. The minister did discuss a comparison between the rates from the prairies to Vancouver as against the rates from the prairies to Fort William, and he said -
I said that the comparison was unfair, not because it was a paper rate but because the grain at the head of the lakes was still inland and had to go a thousand miles.

I agree with the minister, and that is my point. I contend that you are building up a discrimination in freights against the open ports of the Pacific inasmuch as geographically you are compelled to have the grain locked up for several months. But why should we suffer the inequalities in this freight rate structure merely because we have been given by providence certain ports which are open the year round?
The next point made by the Minister of Railways was this-and here he went off at a tangent-that the rates are now the lowest in the west, that the railways could not maintain equipment, that there would be increased unemployment and greater taxation if they forced to lower their rates still further. He also said that the Canadian Pacific Railway in 1934 had barely earned its interest on its bonds. Let us analyze the significance of that argument. Vancouver, Prince Rupert and Alberta are to be discriminated against because the railways of Canada are facing at the present time a severe financial stringency. But, I submit, why should we be the ones to suffer as a result of the financial conditions in which the railways of Canada find themselves to-day? Should not this be the proper course? Should we not in the first place establish a uniform system of equity and justice in the freight rate structure of the country, and then on that basis of equity of contribution and sacrifice do everything possible to assist both the privately owned railway and the public system?

On the
basis of my hon. friend's argument, the estab-lisment of an equitable base, would he be willing as a first step to scrap the Crowsnest rates?

My hon. friend as usual is trying to draw a red herring across the trail. I think that one of the greatest tasks ahead of some government in the future is to establish for the first time in Canadian history a scientific freight rate structure, because the entire structure as it

Railway Act-Rates on Grain
exists to-day is lopsided, having been built up from the point of view of sectional interests since confederation-concessions here and concessions there. From our point of view we can prove that there has been the rankest discrimination against us in the west from the operation of the freight rate system of Canada as we have it now.
The fourth point made by my hon. friend is the very old and ineffective argument, that construction costs were exceedingly heavy in the Rocky mountains while local business was small, therefore we in the far west must pay the penalty of our geography. I do not believe that argument is based on fundamental justice. All that my hon. friend from New Westminster wants, all that the people of British Columbia are asking for, irrespective of party, is that there shall be applied to this question the fundamental principles of simple justice. My hon. friend's next point was that the board of railway commissioners was pretty much a sacrosanct institution, that it had always been successful in its decisions and that appeals against it had failed; therefore, according to my hon. friend, we should look to it as the court of last resort. They had ruled against the contention of my hon. friend from New Westminster and therefore they were the court of last resort.

My hon. friend is not fair. I did not say that because they ruled against the hon. gentleman's contention we should therefore accept them as the final authority. I said that all governments had accepted their rulings, in practically all of forty-five cases.

I accept my hon. friend's amendment. But these are days of new deals, especially in the ministry to which the hon. gentleman belongs. But even granting that in the past governments have accepted with a degree of finality the judgment of the board of railway commissioners in these matters, surely my hon. friend must recognize that to-day we are endeavouring to meet new conditions, and we are appealing for justice to be meted out to the west and particularly to British Columbia.
The final point made by the minister was one that was not worthy of him, if I may say so in all kindness. He said that if we were sitting where he is now, inside of two or three months-and we certainly shall-and we were confronted with the same problem, we might feel a certain degree of embarrassment if my hon. friend from New Westminster should bring up the question again. Let me say to the minister that those of us who come from British Columbia, and possibly this will apply to my hon. friends from that province sitting
on the other side of the house, regardless of the issue of the next election, intend to continue to fight to see that justice is done our province and Alberta and western Canada generally with respect to this question of freight rates, which at the present time works the cruelest discrimination against the whole Pacific coast and the western plains of this dominion.

I wish to say a word or two in support of this bill. I introduced the same subject many years ago, not perhaps by way of a bill but by way of a resolution and when the estimates were under consideration. I introduced it a number of times before the hon. member who sponsors this bill came to the house, but when I found that he attacked the injustice with so much vigour and energy I was glad to leave the matter in his capable hands. The hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Chaplin) has asked how long this injustice has continued. I can recall the time when he sat in the opposition for a number of years-and when you are in opposition is the time to be virtuous-^and I cannot remember his ever lending the weight of his influence and his voice to support the cause when I urged it. I know he has a good memory because he has checked me up more than once, and if he supported me on those occasions I shall be glad to be corrected. I cannot remember however that he ever did so.
The Minister of Railways (Mr. Manion), in opposing this bill, has made allusion to appeals to the privy council, otherwise the cabinet. The Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) discussing this matter some years ago, said that it was not a wise tning, the arrangement that existed of taking appeals to the privy council, because it was taking them to a body whom he termed politicians, a political body, and he gave reasons to show how it had originated in that way. He said the arrangement was no longer desirable, and with that I agree to some extent, as I did then. But I suggested then, as I suggest now, that the proper appeal should be to the exchequer court where it would not be considered by a political body and there would be none of the dangers attending an appeal of that sort.
The minister said that this parliament was not a rate making body. May I point out that we passed a vital act dealing with Crows-nest rates in 1923 or 1924. Then he speaks about its being undesirable to interfere with it because it is such a complicated structure. But who asks him to change the structure? We are merely asking him to remedy an obvious injustice, something which is so
Railway Act-Rates on Grain

obvious that a schoolboy can see the logic of it. We do not propose to tear down the whole structure; that is not suggested. Perhaps I might give an analogous illustration. If my wife asked me to fix a screen door on which one of the hinges was lose, needing a nail and I said, "Woman, I cannot possibly build a house," the obvious answer to that would be, "It will be time enough to talk about building a house when you are asked to build one; in the meantime the hinge needs to be fixed and can be fixed." But there is one thing in all the arguments-and I have heard a great many in the last fourteen years-and it is this. I have never heard anything said really to justify the existence of the differential between the export rate and the domestic rate. Attempts have been made to cover it up, to sidetrack it, but I have never heard an attempt made to justify it. The minister spoke about the heavy snowfalls causing increased transportation costs on grain going through the Rocky mountains, but snow falls on the just and unjust alike; it falls on trains carrying export as well as domestic wheat. Therefore that argument in favour of a differential is quite absurd.

I was only pointing out
the high cost of operation in the mountains. If the hon. member will take my arguments and deal properly with them, I have no objection; but I do object to his twisting my statements. I said that operating costs were higher in the mountains than on the prairies.
Why did my hon. friend say that if he did not use it as an argument?
My hon. friend from New Westminster in his speech had argued as to the low grades and cheap operating costs in some sections of the mountains. I used the argument as contra to that.
Then they were both illogical, as the cost does not affect the differential.

There is only one logical
man in the house, I suppose.

There is, I am glad to say,
generally one person right in an argument. The minister spoke about the cabinet not being in a position to handle this question. I quite frankly admit that the cabinet is not the best body to handle it on an appeal, but the cabinet have given an illustration of what in part they have already done, and they could do this: they could put pressure on the railway companies to reduce the differential not only to the extent they have already done it-for they have only cut it in half
fMr. Neill.1
and at present this applies merely to No. 4 tough wheat and coarse grains and lower- but if they could apply it to No. 2 tough and lower and all mill feeds a good deal of this trouble would be eliminated. There is no justification whatever for making this apply to some grades of wheat and not making it apply to mill feeds. I believe mill feeds were originally left out more or less by a misunderstanding than on account of anything else.
The minister says that the railways might lose money and curtail their services to the people. He does not need to worry about that because I am credibly advised that the putting on of that reduced rate resulted in increased traffic that was profitable to the railway companies, as the rate is still much higher than the export rate; and I will diefy anyone to say that the export rate is not profitable to the railways, otherwise they would not be so keenly competing with each other to get the traffic. Therefore it is profitable for the railways to carry export grain at a fixed rate, and consequently it must be profitable for them to carry domestic grain, which does not cost any more to haul and which is of less value, at a price something less than double the export rate. If the minister could use his influence-and he can because he has used it already and the Prime Minister has used his-to have this rate apply to No. 2 tough wheat and lower and coarse grains and mill feeds, it would meet a great deal of the complaint this bill seeks to remedy.

I
listened with a great deal of interest to the speech of the Minister of Railways (Mr. Manion) and with rather less to some of the speeches that followed. The minister suggested that perhaps railway rates to-day are antiquated. They may be, but the man that undertakes to revise and redraft railway rates in this country is undertaking a pretty big task. There is no possible doubt that Canadian export rates are to-day the lowest in the world and are not made on any reasonable scientific method of providing the railways with adequate revenue for the work which they perform. Roughly our export rates are about fifty-five per cent of the United States rates for like distances or like commodities; that is a fact which cannot be successfully controverted. If the Canadian National Railways were able to-day to get the rates that are extorted by United States and continental roads, not only would they show a surplus, but with that surplus they would be able practically to rebuild their entire motive power and their rolling

Railway Act-Rates on Grain
stock as well. I am quite satisfied that any hon. member who gives close study to the matter and looks into the whole structure of railway rates in this country for the last twenty or thirty years will bear me out in the conclusions I have reached. I know of no branch of industry in Canada that has a poorer showing for its investment for the energy and ability with which it has been managed, than has our railway system.

I do not know whether I have time at my disposal this evening to deal with all the arguments which have been advanced by the Minister of Railways (Mr. Manion) against this bill, which I have introduced now for the fourth time. At the outset he spoke about the House of Commons not being the proper place for rate making. Were I bringing up the general question of freight rates in the house, there might be some force in his argument, but I am not doing that; I am asking parliament to give British Columbia what parliament in 1925 gave for all grain traffic going to Fort William, a rate which had been in existence since 1897. The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Hanson) interrupted to ask whether we would care to advocate. the abrogation of the Crowsnest pass rate. No, we are asking: Give us the Crowsnest pass rate. When speaking the other day I said that the government would not dare to abrogate that rate.
Have you not the Crowsnest pass rate on export grain now?

I contend that we have not. It is still two or three cents higher if you take the actual mileage, but I a>m not bringing up that point just now; I am asking that the domestic rate be the same as the Crowsnest pass rate.
That is a different matter, but you have the Crowsnest pass rate at the present time on export grain.

That is a debatable point, but I am not going into that because I am dealing with grain for domestic purposes in British Columbia and I am asking that that grain be given the Crowsnest pass rate.
As regards the minister's remarks about export rates 'being competing rates, might I point out that argument has been advanced many times by the railroads, but when it suits they are very good at changing their ground. When we quote certain rates to them, they have other excuses to offer. When we said that the domestic rate from Fort William to Montreal was twenty-five cent6
and the export rate was thirtyJour and a half cents, they had no answer to give. Let me point this out to the house; the railways have never shown that export rates at present in existence from Calgary or Edmonton to Vancouver mean a loss to them. I maintain that the rate of twenty cents is a paying rate and two of the members of the board of railway commissioners say the same thing. If that rate is a paying one, why should we in British Columbia for the grain we use have to pay one hundred per cent more than do our competitors in other lands? It is no wonder that at one time the people of British Columbia were seriously thinking of buying Canadian grain in lapan or England and bringing it into that province. There was a time in 1934 when Canadian grain, Nos. 2, 3 and 4, could be purchased in Yokohama, lapan, and brought into the Fraser valley at twenty-five cents a ton cheaper than the price at which it could be brought in from the prairies. I was one of those who advocated that we do this and thus prove the utter absurdity of charging us forty-one and a half cents a hundred pounds for inferior grain when our competitors in Japan could purchase the same or higher grades at a much cheaper rate.
The minister spoke about the United States rates, but he was not exactly fair in that. I have before me the whole rate structure as presented by the railway companies in the appeal last fall. I shall take the time to dispute the statement made by the minister, even if the discussion has to continue at the next sitting. Take the case of Cut Bank, Montana, 732 miles. It is true the old domestic rate was 384 for wheat as against 414 for our domestic rate. I admit that tariff No. 145 is now 304, but the Minister of Railways ignored entirely the fact that there is another rate for coarse grains.
In the United States?
Yes.
I apologize for interrupting, but I think my hon. friend is wrong.
These are figures presented by the railways before the board of railway commissioners. A copy was given to me by counsel.
Will the hon. gentleman read the rates?

Yes, I shall take Shelby, Montana: distance, 757 miles; old domestic rate, 384; coarse grains, 344. Now, 344 for coarse grains and mill feed is considerably better than 414-
Railway Act-Rates on Grain
But it is not as cheap as our rate on low grade grain at the present time.

The trouble with the minister is that he is not conversant with feed requirements. In the Fraser valley, and I suppose in other farming districts where they keep cows and chickens, mill feeds represent fifty per cent of the requirements.
More.

I did not say it was a
paper rate from Montreal to the maritimes; I said from the head of the lakes to Montreal.

The last time this item was up for consideration I asked if the minister had an estimate of the value of the work done by the men in the National Defence unemployment relief camps. At that time I believe he said he had an estimate, and I should like him to give me the figures.

Supply-Defence-Relief Camps

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
The hon. member has
asked for the expenditures on relief camps?
No; I asked for the value of the work done by the men in the National Defence unemployment relief camps.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
I have the estimated
value of the work done up to September 30, 1934. It is based on an average efficiency of relief personnel of fifty per cent, and the figure is given as $6,747,331. The total man days of relief afforded to that date was 7,569,199.
Is that for the whole of Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Yes.

Is the twenty cents per
day allowed the men in the relief camps paid on days when the weather is not fit for the men to work?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
If the men go out at
all to work they receive the allowance.
If the weather is so bad that they cannot leave the camps they are not paid the allowance?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Under those circumstances they do not receive the allowance.

Some little time ago
about forty men were arrested for getting relief under false pretences. I believe they went into the camps under assumed names. Who authorized the arrests? Was it the Department of National Defence?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Could the hon. member give me some further information in the matter?
Some of the arrests took place in the city of Vancouver, and some of them in other British Columbia camps.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext: When?

Approximately three
weeks ago.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I am without information with regard to the matter. I do not recollect anything of the sort coming before the Department of National Defence.

In years gone by we have
protested about the inadequate allowance given by the government to the young men who are forced to go into the relief camps and to accept twenty cents a day or about $5 a month. I was glad) to observe the government saw fit to bring in a measure providing for a minimum wage, and as a result of which I hope before long we will have a national minimum wage in effect.

In the event of the minimum wage law becoming effective will the Department of National Defence live up to government regulations and pay these men in the camps the minimum wage prescribed in their legislation?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I believe the hon. member is referring to a discussion which took place on a previous occasion when this estimate was before the committee. The hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power) raised the same point. I believe these hon. members have failed to realize that the handling of relief is as a result of arrangements made between the federal and provincial governments after the provinces had asked the dominion for assistance. By agreement the dominion took over the care of the single homeless unemployed men and stipulated that in certain places throughout Canada camps should be erected in which those men could find work to do. In the event of the men accepting the work provided they were to receive certain food, clothing and shelter, plus an allowance of twenty cents per day. By agreement with the provinces that was undertaken, and the men who choose to comply with the regulations obtain work and receive the returns.

That does not answer my question. As I said before, in years gone by several of us in this part of the house have protested against the totally inadequate allowance given by the government to these young men who are compelled by force of circumstances and through no fault of their own to go into these relief camps. Now that we are trying to bring about better social conditions throughout the country and improve the lot of the under dog I think it would be an appropriate time for the government to step in and give to these young men who are rendering useful service to the country something more than the twenty cents per day that they are now receiving. I have had many complaints from the camps. I received1 one only this week from a camp somewhere near Hudson, Ontario, along that very line. Men leave the camps often without a cent in their possession because of the very low allowance they receive from the government, and they go out into the world almost penniless. If they are doing work at all they should be paid a proper rate by the government for what they do. I know that many young men are forced by the regulations in some of our municipalities to go into these camps, otherwise they cannot get relief from the municipality. In view of these circumstances, when they are compelled to go into the camp and are forced

Supply-Defence-Relief Camps
to work they should be given more than twenty cents a day.
As I have said, the government contemplates introducing minimum wage legislation, and I am now speaking of the principle of that minimum wage legislation. If we are to adopt the principle of the payment by employers of labour of a minimum wage for services rendered in any part of the dominion, I think one of the first to recognize that principle should be the government themselves; for how can we expect any private employer of labour to accept the principle if right off the bat, so to speak, the government refuse to adopt the very principle which they are responsible for, and for which no doubt they will take so much credit when the time arrives? So my plea to the minister is that he should not only take into serious consideration but act favourably upon the idea of paying to these young men who are in the camps a proper wage for the work they do. That at least would be comforming with the idea the government has in mind in submitting to parliament minimum wage legislation.
Sir EUGENE FI8ET: I wonder if the minister would be kind enough to inform me if he has received a request from the officer commanding Les Fusilliers du Bas-Saint Laurent for an extension of the present headquarters of the armoury at Rimouski and also for the erection of a new armoury at Mont Joli in the county of Rimouski. I think that a recommendation was sent to the general officer commanding the Quebec district and that it wa,s strongly endorsed by him, and the officers of the regiment were rather encouraged by headquarters to believe that the recommendation would be favourably considered and acted upon out of the general relief appropriation.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
I did receive such a communication, and the question is under consideration along with the requests of many other regiments who have made similar applications.
Sir EUGENE FISET. During the last war this regiment under the voluntary system furnished 2,500 men to go overseas, and the bulk of them formed part of the 22nd regiment. It is one of the most deserving units you could possibly find in the whole of Canada, and if the minister could see his way clear to helping them I think it would be rendering a great service to the cause.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I shall be very glad, Mr Chairman, to give the matter full consideration.
May I ask the minister if the twenty cents a day which the men receive in the unemployment relief camps is a wage or an allowance?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext: It is an allowance.
An honorarium.

Then if it is an allowance why is it not paid on the days the men do not work as well as on the days they do work? The men believe it is a wage, and I think there is some logic in their argument. I would ask the .minister to take into consideration recommending to the government that this allowance be paid regardless of whether the men work or not, that is if the man is willing to work. I have a letter here from a young chap in one of these camps, and he says in part, "In the event of the weather being so unfit that we cannot work we lose a day's pay. Yesterday we were not able to work, so we lost twenty cents." Now twenty cents is not a great deal to the minister but it is a great deal to the men in these camps. Circumstances alter oases, and I am sure that if the minister was in the camp at twenty cents a day he would like to get that twenty cents. My correspondent goes on to say,, "Believing that the government would not stop that twenty cents if they knew about it, I am risking writing to you and losing my job in the bargain if caught." I would like to impress on the minister that here is a young chap who still has some faith in the government, and I think the government need's all the faith that is possible in these hard times. I suggest that the government stretch a point here-it is not a very great stretch-and consider giving to these men the allowance regardless of whether the day is fit for work or not. I hope the minister will take that suggestion into consideration.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Certainly. Every suggestion made in this committee will be taken into very serious consideration.
I am always afraid, Mr. Chairman, that when these suggestions are taken into serious consideration they usually go into the waste paper basket.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Oh, no.

I would much prefer that the minister say to my hon. friend from Vancouver South (Mr. Maclnnis), "Yes, we will accede to your very modest request. " After I have been asking that these men be paid the minimum wage I am surprised that my hon. friend from Vancouver South should come along with such an exceedingly modest request
Supply-Defence-Relief Camps

as he has made. It has left me almost speechless. I woud seriously ask the minister not to take my hon. friend's request into serious consideration, but here and now to give assent to it so that the men in the camps shall at least be assured of twenty cents a day whether the weather is fine or not.

I almost feel like apologizing to my hon. friend from North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps), but my ancestors were Scotch. I think the minister should give me a definite answer to this very modest-much too modest -request, so that I may have a reply to send to my correspondent.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I suggest that the hon. member reply to his correspondent that on the 22nd of March he brought the matter up in committee of supply and the minister responsible assured him that, just as every suggestion would receive earnest consideration, his would.
And sympathetic consideration?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Yes, and sympathetic consideration.

I want to join my voice to the protests of other hon. members in this corner of the house with respect to this twenty cents a day business. I frankly think it is a disgrace to this country, particularly after all we have heard to-day regarding our wealth and returning prosperity, that this twenty cents a day, this miserable and utterly inappropriate pay, be continued even if it is called an allowance.
But I rose for another purpose, in connection with a complaint that I placed before the minister some time ago in regard to some of the camps out from Calgary. Since taking that matter up I have received from the office of the city clerk of Calgary some correspondence in connection with this case. I find that on February 5 the city clerk, J. M. Miller, wrote a note to his worship Mayor Davison in the following terms:
Dear Sir:
I beg to advise you that council, at its regular meeting held last evening, adopted the following motion:-
"That this council authorize Hi? Worship the Mayor to direct to the attention of dominion and provincial government officials the plight of single men at present in Calgary, formerly of relief camps, requesting that some provision for their maintenance be immediately undertaken and the present situation thereby rectified.
"Further, that an investigation be immediately undertaken by the dominion and provincial governments concerning reported

unsatisfactory conditions at the various relief camps and a report thereon furnished this council."
Kindly give this matter your attention.
Yours truly,
J. M. Miller,
City Clerk.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext: What is the date of that letter?

Februarj' 5. On February 6 the following letter was written by A. Davison, the mayor of Calgary, to the Honourable Wesley Gordon, Minister of Labour, Ottawa, Canada:
Dear Sir:
The following resolution was passed by our city council at its regular meeting on February 4th, and I forward same to you for your consideration and action.
"That this council authorize His Worship the Mayor to direct to the attention of dominion and provincial government officials the plight of single men at present in Calgary, formerly of relief camps, requesting that some provision for their maintenance be immediately undertaken and the present situation thereby rectified.
"Further, that an investigation be immediately undertaken by the dominion and provincial governments concerning reported unsatisfactory conditions at the various relief camps and a report thereon furnished this council."
A considerable number of single men are now drifting into Calgary from the various camps, and we are fearful unless some action is taken that a serious, situation may develop locally. Your early attention to this matter will be much appreciated.
Yours very truly,
A. Davison,
Mayor.
The last paragraph had been added by the mayor. On February 20 the following letter was sent by J. M. Miller, city clerk, to Brigadier General D. W. B. Spry:
Dear Sir:
The council, at its regular meeting held with date of February 18th, had before it for consideration clause 1 of the report of the city commissioners' dated February 15th, and which concerns reported complaints to the council respecting single men's camps. A copy of the clause refered to, together with the correspondence referred to therein, is attached for your information.
In dealing with the matter the council instructed that the various features referred to in the reports of the investigating officers be directed to your attention and with a recommendation that better water supply be afforded, better recreational features furnished, that the men be permitted to formulate committees for the purpose of presenting their grievances, and if at all possible, that permission be granted the men to come to the city at times within reason.

Sup-ply-Defence-Relief Camps
Might I respectfully request that after the council's representations in this respect have received your attention that I might receive your report thereon.
Yours truly,
J. M. Miller,
City Clerk.
On February 22, Brigadier General D. W. B. Spry wrote to the mayor as follows:
Dear Mr. Mayor:
Receipt is acknowledged of the communication from the city clerk of February 20, 1935, attaching the correspondence of the city commissioner and the reports of the gentlemen you asked permission for to visit the Department of Rational Defence camps in the Kananaskis valley.
It does not appear to be clear to your committee re the point raised1 in regard to water supply, that these camps were under construction and final completion of wash houses had not been completed. Further, that it is the policy that all these camps are constructed by the men themselves. During construction it is only normal that improvised systems have to be employed. The water supplies are now practically all completed, leaving no further grounds for reasonable complaints.
In regard to recreational facilities, as you are no doubt aware a recreational hut is supplied by the department, but that all equipment, such as books, games, radios, gramophones, et cetera, are obtained from private subscriptions, in which the citizens of Calgary have assisted very materially, and the profits from men's canteens:	mostly, however, by
private efforts as canteen profits are of necessity small. Should your council feel inclined to assist us in this work by a grant for camps in the vicinity of Calgary, or to which Calgary men are admitted, it would 'be very greatly appreciated.
With regard to the method of registering complaints, the following are the regulations in this respect as laid down by the Department of National Defence for all camps in the dominion:
"The following rules regarding complaints will be observed:
(a)	One of the fundamental and most necessary rules for the administration of unemployment relief camps is to forbid anything bearing the appearance of combination to obtain redress of alleged grievances. Appeals for redress by means of any document bearing the signature of more than one complainant, or by organized committees combining to make a complaint are strictly forbidden.
(b)	If any man has a complaint or accusation to bring against a member of the supervisory or administrative staff, such complaint should be laid before the camp foreman, who, if necessary, will transmit it to district headquarters or camp superintendent.
(c)	If the camp foreman neglects or refuses to attend to a complaint, the complainant may bring the matter to the notice of the district headquarters or camp superintendent.
(d)	The department will not countenance any steps to bring accusations before the tribunal of public opinion, either by speeches, or letters inserted in the newspapers, by men actively employed on relief work. Such a
proceeding is a glaring violation of the rules and shows a contempt for properly constituted authority.
(e)	It is the duty of the camp foreman to investigate all complaints and, when receiving complaints for transmission to superior authority, to point out to the parties concerned any irregularity in the means they 'employ in seeking redress. In hearing complaints or statements, et cetera, camp foremen are advised to invariably have another member of the supervisory staff present as a witness to all proceedings. The complaint, when forwarded to district headquarters oir camp superintendent, is to be accompanied by a statement and recommendation, if any, of the camp foreman.
(f)	No 'application or complaint should ever be -made to the civil power, except through the camp foreman or with his sanction."
Trusting the above is the information you require.
Yours truly,
D. W. B. Spry,
Brigadier General, D.O.C., M.D. No. 13.
I have never heard of any such document outside of an internment camp during war time.
That would be in the army.

The army is about the only place where you might expect such a suppression of individual and private rights. I resent this and I protest to the minister and to the government that these men should have the right to organize their complaint committees. I believe this government would be- well advised to permit within the camps the form of self-government which is permitted within our universities.
The right of assembly.

At least the right of assembly to secure redress of wrongs. This is a violation of every decent law of British justice and practice, and the fact that such a Prussian-like document is presented as the official rules regulating a camp in Canada is certainly an indication of the ruthless -character of the system which has thrust these men into the camps as the only means of escaping their misery and starvation. I want to make my protest in this matter as forceful as I can, and I repeat the words of Brigadier General Spry, as follows :
One of the fundamental and most necessary rules for the administration of unemployment relief camps is to forbid anything bearing the appearance of combination to obtain redress of alleged grievances. Appeals for redress by means of any document bearing the signature of more than one complainant or by organized committees combining to make a complaint are strictly forbidden.
Supply-Defence-Relief Camps

What kind of men are these with whom we are dealing? Are they brutal men? Are they revolutionary? Are they not Canadian citizens who through no fault of their own are in this terribly unhappy condition? Surely the minister himself is sufficiently British in his instincts, a sufficiently good sportsman to understand that this is not sportsmanship. It is not even decency; it is sheer Prussian oppression. Under subsection (d) we find:
The department will not countenance any steps-
Note that; the department will not countenance any steps.

to bring accusations before the tribunal of public opinion.
And so we have turned these relief camps definitely into military secret camps where the most rigid discipline-yes, more rigid than in war time, even worse than the discipline which the soldiers had to undergo-is carried out. These men are under more rigid discipline than is necessary for the maintenance of armed forces.	[DOT]
Will the hon. member repeat the date?,
February 22, 1935.
Are you sure it isn't 1535?

I am not so sure about that; it might be under Cromwell. The department, we are told, will not countenance any steps to bring accusations before the tribunal of public opinion.
-either by speeches or letters inserted in the newspapers by men actively employed on relief work.
Employed?

Yes; "employed" is good in view of the discussion which we have had.
Such a proceeding is a glaring violation of the rules and shows a contempt for properly constituted authority.
The writing of a letter to my hon. friend here is a flouting of properly constituted authority, and so is the making of a speech in Calgary or in a camp or anywhere else.
Or in parliament.
Well, we are not on relief yet.
Not yet is right.
There is no civil authority.

As to the replies received from the department, I have

the following report to make. I asked the question:
Have men been ejected from this camp for having registered complaints?
The reply from the department was a categorical denial in the form of a negative-no. I at once took this matter up witih my correspondents in Calgary and I am informed that the reply to the question, to use their own language and not my own, is "an absolute lie." They say:
Our committee have dealt 'with innumerable cases and this was confirmed by the foreman on our visit by the delegates.
In other words, men have been ejected for registering complaints, according to these people who have actually discussed the matter with the foreman. Moreover, when men are dismissed from camps we are told that adequate clothing is left them. On leaving the camp, I am informed, the men have to hand in all the .clothing that they received on loan, except bare necessities. In the provincial camps, those operated by the provincial government, the clothing becomes the property of the man if he remains in camp for thirty days, but in the dominion camp the clothing is always lent and has to be restored as soon as the man leaves the camp or is discharged therefrom. I asked another question:
Are men who have been ejected from one camp under this department refused entrance into any other camp?
I received from the department, signed by the deputy minister, this reply:
Yes, unless the district officer commanding is satisfied that there is reasonable probability of their behaving properly in future.
I am informed that there is not a single instance, in connection with these particular camps, of a man who, having been discharged from one camp, was ever permitted to enter another under this department at any time, certainly never under the name by which he had been employed previously. This is the information that has come to me and I am passing it on to the minister in the hope that he will take the matter up. In subsection (f) of Brigadier General Spry's document of war I find this:
No application or complaint should ever be made to the civil power except through the camp foreman or with his sanction.
After all these people might as well be Armenians under the care of the Turks of old when they are so ruthlessly bereft of every civil liberty, every decency -which we ought to expect among men. They cannot assemble to make their complaints vocally

Supply-Defence-Relief Camps
in the proper way, nor may they write letters to the press, and they are not allowed to make public speeches. They must submit themselves utterly to t'he discipline, the rigorous military discipline of the relief camp. Is it any wonder that the city of Calgary has put on record two resolutions under date March 7, following the discussion we had previously in this house on this very question? The covering letter to myself reads:
Calgary, Canada, March 7, 1935. Mr. E. J. Garland, M.P.,
House of Commons,
Ottawa, Canada.
Dear Sir:
Re: Single men's relief camps as operated by the Department of National Defence
For your information and attention I beg to enclose herewith copies of resolutions adopted by the city council from time to time, together with copies of correspondence which has taken place between responsible officials in this above connection.

"That council's previous action, together with copy of regulations governing camps, as furnished by Brigadier Spry, in respect of complaints re single men's relief camps, be directed to the attention of the Right Hon. the Prime Minister of Canada and Dr. G. D. Stanley, M.P., with a request that our recommendations be carried out.
Further, that copies of resolutions and' correspondence in this connection be forwarded to Mr. E. J. Garland, member for Bow River riding, with a request that the matter also receive his attention."
May I respectfully request, on behalf of the council, that the various matters receive your attention and consideration and that I be furnished with your reply thereto at the earliest convenience.

City Clerk.
The first resolution reads:
That this council authorize His Worship the Mayor to direct to the attention of dominion and provincial government officials the plight of single men at present in Calgary, formerly of relief camps, requesting that some provision for their maintenance be immediately undertaken and the present situation thereby rectified.
Further, that an investigation be immediately undertaken by the dominion and provincial governments concerning reported' unsatisfactory conditions at the various relief camps and a report thereon furnished this council.
Evidently the conditions are still unsatisfactory, and I would sincerely ask the minister to have a further investigation made into the whole question. This is the other resolution:
That the various features brought out in the report of the reporting officers before this council, re single men's relief camps, be referred to the proper authorities in an endeavour tc have better water supply afforded, better recreational features,-
Evidently the report was not satisfactory.

permission to the men to formulate their complaint committees to present their grievances and to permit of the men coming to the city at least within reason. That a report on these matters be received by this council from the proper authorities.
I have not much more to say on this matter other than to convey to the minister this paragraph from a letter received from the United Workers' Council of Delegates of Calgary under date of February 20:
When a man is fired in the afternoon and no transport available he has to remain in camp until next morning, then he has to pay fifteen cents for breakfast.
After the munificent remuneration or honorarium of twenty cents a day has been paid.
The men are given transport to Seebe crossing and then told to fend for themselves. This means that they must walk two miles to the highway or risk their lives by boarding a freight, and they can then be picked up for breaking the law. When these men come into Calgary we always try to get them sent to a provincial camp, but they bring out records and I can assure you they have all . their records except finger prints, and' about the most they can find against these men is that they are not satisfied with their conditions, and we believe they have every reason to be dissatisfied when they get a miserable pay of twenty cents a day for a day's work.
Last October we had thirty men in from Coleman and the following facts were brought out in the police court here when nineteen men were given thirty days in Lethbridge for obtaining a meal without means to pay for same.
1.	The men rvere transported to Frank and then told to board a freight to Calgary.
2.	The camp foreman Captain Coates fired the men on the advice of the straw boss without questioning the men whatsoever.
3.	The men were fired for complaining and' organizing and the camp rules forbid organizations for the purpose of adjusting grievances.
4.	Most of these boys had never been inside a police court before and the magistrate said he must punish them or many more men would leave the camps for the cities.
From a moral standpoint the camps should be abolished, but until they are able to do this they should at least pay a day's pay for a day's . work and then a man could at least be able to leave the environment of the camps and come to the cities for recreation once in a while.
