E. Le Vesionte,
Secretary-Treasurer.
I think I have given enough to the minister to justify my asking him once more, first of all without any further investigation to grant to these men the right of organizing their complaint committees. That is not too much to ask. These men are not criminals; they are not in penitentiaries. We are treating them as though they were, and this is not right. They should be given the right of protesting when they feel justified in doing so, and they should be permitted to organize in order to present their complaints in a proper fashion. Let them have an authorized and well known complaints committee in each camp; let them elect their men by popular ballot within the camp; let the chairman of the complaints committee be in touch with the local foreman or supervisor, and let him be recognized as spokesman for the men. If the minister will do these things, he will have much less trouble and the men themselves wlil be much better satisfied.

The conditions described by the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland) are certainly appalling, and1 I sincerely hope the ministelr will give some satisfactory explanation and will repudiate the sentiments expressed in the letter from the commanding officer at Calgary. Those men, as my hon. friend says, are not criminals; they are working in the camps. They are on relief possibly through no fault of their own, and to say that they cannot give voice to complaints and expose their grievances is taking away from them the right which belongs to every Canadian citizen; they are not being treated like human beings. When they work in the relief camps they are not in penal institutions. I join my protest to that expressed by the hon. member for Bow River, and if the policy which is 'formulated by the commanding officer at 'Calgary is the one which prevails in all the other camps under the minister's department, I say that it is an insult to Canadian dignity and even to manhood.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
The hon. member for Bow River started by referring to a resolution which was passed by the city council of Calgary on February 4 and which I believe was transmitted to Ottawa. On February 7, presumably by direction of the mayor or the city council of Calgary, the medical health officer for that city visited the camps referred to, and I propose to read to the committee the report which he submitted to his worship the mayor of the city of Calgary on February 8:

Dear Sir,-As instructed by you, yesterday accompanied by Mr. Cowey of this department and representatives from the United Workers' Council of Delegates, I conducted a sanitary survey of the camps established by the dominion government, Department of National Defence, under project No. 155. These camps have been established, I take it, for the express: purpose of clearing up undergrowth and thinning out trees in connection with activities of the forestry 'department. There are four camps: Seebe, Lusk Creek, Eau-Claire, and Barrier, and it is assumed that these camps will-at capacity-take care of 138 men in each camp. They are at the present time separate units, all under the supervision of Mr. Armstrong who officiates in the capacity of resident engineer. Visits were made to the four camps and I have the following to report:
The camps are situated on high, dry locations and I think the sites very well chosen, having regard to access of water and general satisfactory surroundings. They consist of huts in Which the men are housed; kitchen and dining rooms', bath house, stores, blacksmith shop, garages, and administrative office. It would appear that in the Seebe camp the aim is to house twelve men in each but. This, in so far as cubic capacity is concerned would be quite satisfactory but I might here suggest that possibly a much more satisfactory purpose would be served by limiting the capacity to ten men, having regard to the perforce location of the stove, tables and such like designed for the comfort of the men. It must be thoroughly understood that these camps were not organized until late in November, 1934, and: consequently, structural matters have not yet reached completion. In the three other camps other than Seebe camp, there is up to the present time makeshift bath or wash houses. This condition, whilst resulting in some inconvenience is rapidly being remedied. The bath houses presently under construction (and: which I was assured would be finished very shortly) are complete with shelves upon which aTe several wash basins and there are five showers. The shelves and the floor and walls of the showers are lined with galvanized iron and properly drained. Water is being laid on and from the layout I -would say would be adequate. Pumps, storage tanks, heaters and necessary plumbing for the bath houses -and kitchens are in process of completion and I think will result in a very nice situation. Washing machines are provided and adequate hot and cold water is to be supplied.
The kitchens and dining rooms were scrupulously clean; crockery ware is provided instead of enamel ware; dining tables are covered with white oilcloth and some of the kitchen tables are covered with galvanized iron. The quality of the cutlery is such that, in my mind, bids for a most attractive atmosphere. The party had the privilege of eating lunch at Seebe camp and indulged in the routine bill of fare. Personally I am all for it; the food was very nice, well cooked, ample and plain and sustaining withal. The kitchen equipment is practically all new; stoves, equipment and stores were perfectly clean. Kitchen waste is disposed of in gravel leaching pits; new pits are dug as required. The storage of meat is taken care of in usual camp manner by hanging from trees. Store houses and root cellars are being erected and ice is to be provided to care for perishable foodstuffs.

Supply-Defence-Relief Camps
The stores are well stocked with clothing and the men are furnished with new clothing by submitting that which is worn out. The clothing is designed for comfort and service.
It is the intention to provide a recreation hut and canteen facilities. Construction of this is completed in Seebe camp. For a time it is thought that profits from the canteen will go to purchase a radio for each of the four camps. _
The -water supply is from the Kananaskis river or wells, depending on the location of the camp, and in the last or Barrier camp, from a spring emanating from Barrier mountain. It is understood that this spring has formed the bone of contention, but I cannot see where there is any ground for complaint in this respect. There is an abundance of water and it is hoped to intercept the spring at a higher level and bring the water to the camp by gravity. All water supplies are obviously of the pure type.
It was suggested that some difficulty had obtained in having adequate water supply for bathing purposes in the past. I cannot see that this complaint is justified, for each camp approximates an adequate supply of water and, in the event of anybody wanting to take a bath, it would be only a matter of a few minutes to obtain water for such a purpose.
The Barrier camp is not as near completion as the other three. It was established on 20th December, 1934, and, therefore is right in the midst of construction activities.
I was given to understand that all four camps are to be of the same type and with the same facilities and conveniences. There is an abundant supply of firewood; the men are not required to take care of their own huts, other men being detailed for this service. There are men on night duty to attend to fires and maintain heat in the huts whilst the rest of the men are sleeping.
Toilet_ facilities are adequate; they are of the privy pit type, of good construction and adequately supplied with toilet paper.
To conclude I feel that at the present time, and allowing for present conditions, these men live under as near ideal surroundings as could be created. I asked as to the work required of them and was assured by several of them- to quote their own words-"there is nothing to it."
Medical attention is provided by a physician from Exshaw who visits all the camps. ' There is also a first-aid man on duty at each camp.
Respectfully submitted,
W. H. Hill,
Medical Officer of Health.
Doctor Hill is the medical officer of the city of Calgary, and this is his opinion, as a medical man, of the condition under which these men live and work. With regard to the complaint so strongly expressed by my hon. friend from Bow River (Mr. Garland), I would repeat that all the arrangements, the work in the camps, the living conditions, and what they have to do if they desire to receive this shelter, food, sustenance and allowance, is laid down and explained to the men. It was arrived at by arrangement between the dominion government and the provincial government; in this case the Alberta government signed the agreement under which these regulations are accepted. If the men do not consider that they are conditions under which they desire to live, they can leave. We had the instance referred to a few evenings ago by the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Barber) of a fit, husky young man aged twenty-five, who had boasted that he had not done any work and had no intention of starting now. In these camps are men of every description. There are men who desire to conform to the arrangements laid down and who are working happily under them. I myself have visited many of the camps. We have had representations from all types of citizens from all parts of Canada giving their opinion of the conditions under which these men live and work; they are satisfied with them. But of course in a body of men of such numbers, and under conditions such as we are passing through in this country-yes, and in the world-there is bound to be a certain number of trouble makers, and it is to endeavour to handle the trouble makers that we safeguard ourselves by the regulations laid down.
Mr. GRAY; Does the minister then approve of the letter of Brigadier General Spry?

agitators are coming into the camps for the purpose of stirring up trouble, the arrangements to deal with these agitators must be such as will properly handle them. If the man is not satisfied with the reply he receives from the foreman, it is perfectly proper that he should go to the superintendent. There is no doubt therefore that the complaints made by the individual reach headquarters and are there considered. But the regulations laid down have been arrived at by agreement between the dominion and the provinces, and the regulations must stand.

I am sorry the minister did not read the letter from the other delegate who also visited the camps. I am sure it was an oversight on his part. Let me, however, touch for a moment on his closing words. He referred to a young man, cited by the hon. member for Fraser Valley, a man twenty-five years of age, who, according to the statement, said he had never worked and never would work. A shame, of course. But does the minister overlook the fact that that boy was just past nineteen when this depression hit him and he could not get a job? After all when one has been out of a job four or five years in the formative period of life, when indelible impressions are made, is it any wonder that he has become embittered against society if it has nothing more to offer him than relief camps? I need make no excuse for him, but it is a wonder that there are not more like him. Let me say that the reason I asked the minister to permit the formation of recognized complaints committees, in touch with the foremen all the time, was to prevent the very danger he foresaw, that of agitators getting in and undermining the morale of these men who under present conditions have no proper outlet for their complaints. The minister says they may complain to the foreman. Let me give him a statement that I have from these people who have investigated the matter.
Who are they?

I shall tell you in a moment.
The foreman stated that he only saw one man at a time with a complaint, and that man was invariably fired. The superintendent stated he never overrode a foreman's decision. We (the United Workers' Council Delegates, of Calgary), have handled hundreds of cases of men fired or quit, and as yet have not met with one who has had a chance to appeal to military district 13. Our delegations have appealed several times to military district 13 for these men to be reinstated, but on each occasion have been met with blank refusal and we have eventually got them accepted by the provincial relief commission.

So much for that statement, I now turn to the report of the other delegate. He received permission to visit the camp at the same time, and in company with Doctor Hill. Hon. members will note that Doctor Hill, according to the minister's statement, was to report on the sanitary conditions. I have raised no complaint, nor do these men raise any complaint about the sanitary conditions in the camp. They are complaining about the Prussian character of the discipline'-the un-British type of discipline.
They want the right to complain.

The second report is as follows:
Labour Temple,
229 Eleventh Ave. East,
Calgary, Alberta,

A. Davison, Esquire,
Mayor, City of Calgary.
Your Worship:
Following up my visit to Seebe with Doctor Hill I beg to inform you that I found the following conditions:-
Notice how fair the man is, all the way through.
The general complaint was shortage of water, the supply at Seebe camp has to be hauled from the river. A pump and pipe line is being erected, so this difficulty should shortly be overcome; then there will be hot and cold showers available. There were plenty of wash baSiris of a very small shallow type for ablution purposes and a large galvanized tub for bathing and laundry purposes. A new washing machine was available and I was informed that this had been in the store since the camp opened in November last but only produced for use three or four days ago. The wash basins also had been issued late last week.
Upon entering camp men are supposed to get an adequate supply of clothing, some of the men stated they had been in camp three weeks or a month and had not yet received the requisite clothing.
The food was plentiful and' of good quality; the dining rooms were excellently fitted up and comfortable; the wash houses in Lemusk, Eau-Clare and Barrier camps were just marquees and new huts are being erected to replace these. The water supply at the latter camp was just a spring at the foot of the mountain. A hole has been dug and boarded for storage of water but appears totally inadequate.
The authorities appear to be doing the best they can to make the men comfortable, but considerable time is needed yet. There is a first-aid man in charge of the hospital cabin in each camp and a full first-aid kit available. The doctor visits the camp twice a week and men have free access to see him.
The principal complaints were as follows:- The camp foreman refuses to see more than one man on any grievance or complaint. If a man complains he is invariably fired. The superintendent stated that they would allow no

Supply-Defence-Relief Camps
agitators or any organization of any kind. The foreman's word is final and the superintendent never overrides the foreman in a decision.
When fired the men have to hand in their clothing, except bare necessities. They are transported to the level crossing at Seebe and left to fend for themselves. Should transport be available they sometimes give the men a ride to Cochrane and on one occasion to Calgary. There is little or no recreation available and the men would welcome a radio, football, games of any description and particularly a supply of good books.
The pay is twenty cents per day when work has been done. Hours of labour are eight to twelve and one to four-thirty p.m. The foreman stated that a fair day's work was expected for what the men received, and no loafers would be tolerated. In my opinion the trouble has been caused through taking men out to the camps before proper facilities were available, and that the whole of the trouble could have been obliterated if the men had been allowed a proper grievance or camp committee.
Respectfully submitted on behalf of above council,
Fred Peat,
President.
The minister has not made an adequate answer at all. The only -answer he has given is that he personally regrets this tyipe of rigid, penitentiary discipline as necessary in our relief camps. I resent that attitude on the part of the minister. I repeat what I said before: these men are not criminals; they are fellow Canadians. They are men who through no fault of their own are out of work. They are ordinary flesh and blood men born in this country, for the most part, and they deserve to be treated as you would expect to be treated and as I would expect to be treated. They do not deserve to be treated in this way. I protest; that is all I can do.

When was the regulation made? As I understand it this is a departmental regulation, known as letter No. 4, sent from headquarters in Ottawa to all the relief camps in Canada. Am I correct in that? If so, when was it made and by whom?

Then it becomes clear, Mr. Chairman, that this is the work of the Department of National Defence entirely, that instructions have been sent out by that department. They were not included in an order in council or anything of that sort. My hon. friend suggested at the opening of his remarks that this was part of an understanding with the province, but clearly he was mistaken in that view. This is merely a direction by the Department of National Defence and it is quite important that we should know it in a definite wray. If these instructions as expressed in the letter of Brigadier Spry have been submitted to the province of Alberta, there should be a record of that submission, and the minister ought to be able to show that the province has accepted such regulations or instructions. Otherwise I do not think it is fair to say that the provincial government are responsible for instructions such as are conveyed in that letter. If they are not responsible, then it is wholly the work of the National Defence department, and I would implore my hon. friend the minister not to attach his own responsibility to those instructions, but to cancel them as quickly as he can.

On several occasions, if my memory serves me rightly, we were informed that there was no military discipline in these relief camps. In past sessions, if I am not mistaken, that information was given to this house.
Seven times seven at least.

Now we are informed through documentary evidence to-night that there is a most rigid form of military discipline in these relief camps under the jurisdiction of the Department of National Defence. Personally I regret exceedingly that the minister has taken the stand that he has here to-night, and I think that on due reflection probably the minister himself will regret it; for if he upholds what is contained in the document that has been read here to-night it means that he is in favour of suppressing the very liberties of a great section of the younger generation in the Dominion of Canada. I think that the type of person who through no fault of his own is compelled to go into the relief camps ought to be dealt with a little more sympathetically than is evidently the case from the evidence

Supply-Defence-Relief Camps
that has been submitted here to-night, and as many of us have known during the past few months. In many instances all the family connections of these young men have been broken up and the family separated much against their will; these young men are taken away from respectable homes, young boys of eighteen and nineteen, and compelled by economic necessity to become inmates of these camps. When a young boy goes into a relief camp the last thing he ought to be subjected to is that rigid military discipline which it has been disclosed in the communications read to-night exists in the camps.
I think it was a very unfortunate remark the minister made here to-nigbt when he said that if these boys do not like it they can leave. In the first place it is economic necessity that has driven them into these camps, and then after the almost inhuman treatment they received at some of the camps they are told, if they do not like it, to get out. These boys, mostly young men, go into these camps not because they want to, -but because there is no alternative for them. The government provide these cam-ps for the young men, and mind you this is the younger generation of Canadians whom we expect to take our place in the future and help build up a country that is worth while. We have been told, of course, that in some respects they are well treated. I am not going to deny everything that the minister has said in so far as that communication is concerned, but the complaint is not about the sanitary conditions of these camps. The complaint is chiefly against the suppression of those liberties which had the minister himself been in opposition I think he would have been the first to champion if this complaint had been brought to his attention.
What liberties does the hon. member suggest have been withdrawn?

I will read section (f) again:
No application nor complaint should ever be made to the civil power, except through the camp foreman or with his sanction.
In other words, an inmate of one of these camps is deprived of communicating with a newspaper; he is deprived of the right of complaining to the municipal authority, deprived of the right o-f going into the city and speaking of conditions as he has found them; he is deprived of the right of communicating even with a member of parliament.
Or even with his mother.

Possibly that is so as well. What I am complaining about is this. We are putting in these camps the younger generation of Canadians and we might reasonably hope that they would receive their good training in Canadian citizenship, but when they get to the camps they find an iron clad rigid military discipline which hardly al'lo-ws them to call their souls their own, and they have to submit to this for twenty cents a day and their keep. Leaving aside for the moment the amount of money they receive for the services they render, what we are stressing at the moment is the rights and liberties of the individual of which these young men are now being deprived. I would urge upon the minister that in these matters of unemployment and unemployment relief the military authorities should not be allowed to be supreme over the civil authorities or in any way to deprive these young men of their liberties. If I were in the position of the minister and for the first time- a document such as the hon. member for Bow River has read to the house to-night was brought to my attention, I would at once repudiate the document entirely, and not only would I repudiate it, but I would fire clean out of the service the men who are responsible for such a thing. The individual possesses certain rights, and when those who are responsible to the civil authorities send out such a document they must know that it is going to create a feeling of hostility. Apparently they feel that in some way they are superior even to this parliament. No document of that type could stand the scrutiny of any body of honest citizens. For the sake of parliament, for the sake of the minister and for the sake of the young men who are compelled to go to these camps, I think something should be done right now in this house to repudiate entirely the document. The men in these camps should be given a fair chance in life.
Mr. SUTHERLAND I think I should say a few words on this question, as this system of camps was inaugurated while I was head of the Department of National Defence. The minister has sketched the beginning of the movement and indicated why these camps were started. Back in 1931 and 1932 there were a large number of younger citizens who were moving around from one place to another and in many instances were getting into cities which were not their homes. There was considerable difficulty in looking after these young men and in time it became an acute problem. During the summer they were moving around on the trains and there were many accidents. I am told that practically all the hospitals in northern Ontario had some of these young men as patients. This scheme was evolved to give them some
Supply-Defence-Belief Camps

place to go. The camps were not started with the primary idea of giving employment for wages; they were started as a temporary measure to provide comfortable surroundings, clothing and food. The allowance of twenty cents per day which was given was in no sense a wage; it was only a little extra pocket money to buy some of the things which were not issued.
As I say, this scheme was started in 1932 and it wen-t very well for a couple of years and in most of the camps everything is going very well to-day. The former Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe), who spoke on this matter, is familiar, I think, with the situation in his own city and in the camp at Valcartier. To my knowledge there have never been any complaints of this type in connection with that camp. Everything goes along smoothly, and while I was in the department I received many expressions of appreciation from the people down there as to the way in which the department was looking after this great problem. The young men at Valcartier come from a large area in Quebec. There is a large camp at Halifax, at the citadel. This camp has been in operation for about three years and nothing of this kind has occurred. There is a large camp at Petawawa, Ontario, at which there are young men mostly from Montreal. There are two camps at Kingston and other camps in northern Ontario. No complaints of the kind referred to to-night have been heard from the Ontario camps. The hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps) referred . to inhuman treatment, but I do not think that term can be applied to these camps. I do not think there has been anything even approaching inhumanity.
These camps are different from the ordinary labour camps. The men in the ordinary labour camp are hired for some certain purpose and the aim and object of the employer is to get work out of his men. The employees quite rightly and properly ask the right to organize in order that they may present their side of any difference which may arise. In these camps everybody is working with the same end in view. The Department of National Defence has started these camps with the sole object of helping these men. There are not two sides of opinion in the camps. Naturally the men want the best they can get, and when parliament passed the money to provide for such camps, that was the sole object in view. While I was in the department we had trouble at only one camp, the one located at Long Branch near Toronto. This trouble was caused by agitators getting into the camp and trying to create an organiza-
tion where one was not necessary. There was some difficulty for a short time, but I maintain that there has been nothing out of the way in any camp, and especially nothing of the nature referred to to-night.
A committee inspected these particular camps and they admit that the food and surroundings are good. Some complaint was made about the water at one camp, but as I understand it the camp was in process of construction. I think it was said that measures were being taken to deal with the matter. The clothing furnished was the same type of clothing as we all wear, substantial and warm. The food bought for the camps is just as good as we get in the parliamentary restaurant, although it may not be served up with as many frills. The fact that good substantial food is furnished has been borne out by the statements made to-night. I do not think the department can be criticized, because it is only in this particular ease that I have heard of any complaint of this kind. I have heard one of the hon. members for Vancouver bring up matters in connection with the camps in British Columbia, but I think it must be admitted that when you have a number of young men in a camp they are bound to be full of life and vim and will have opinions of their own. This will happen no matter how the camps are run. If the men are warm, if the clothing provided is good and the food substantial, I do not think there can be anything to complain of. The camps are not permanent; it is not as though the .men were going 'to be there for some time and had to build up some system of rights. Instead of having this odium cast upon the department and its officials, I think they are entitled to a great deal of praise for the manner in which they have handled the matter. No one knows better than I do the difficulty and anxiety in connection with this work. I presume that there sure over
20,000	men in the camps in the winter and some 12,000 in the summer.

I do not think that this committee is concerned about the food or clothing or water; that is not the complaint. Of course, when camps are being laid out there is always a little difficulty at the start so far as the water supply is concerned, but that is not the difficulty here. Perhaps my hon. friend would answer this question. Does he know who made these regulations, who issued them, when they were issued and whether or not all the relief camps in Canada are subject to them? If I remember rightly, the document which my hon. friend was good enough to let me look at says:

Supply-Defence-Relief Camps
"The following are regulations as laid down by the Department of National Defence for all camps in the dominion." The question that interests me, and I believe it interests a great many members of the committee, is this: When were these regulations made, by whom and on what authority, and did the minister know about them?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: My hon. friend has been in charge of a department and he knows that if something is done in the department the minister takes responsibility for it; that is his job and he does not fall back upon someone under him and blame that subordinate. While I was in the department I took responsibility for everything that went on there; that was part of my job, and if it was wrong I took responsibility for it. I did not look for someone to put the blame on, and I am sure that my hon. friend knows very well that there have to be regulations in connection with a vast scheme of this kind, where young men are constantly coming into and going out of camps. A ou must have regulations.
How long have these regulations been in force?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: They were in force before a single man was ever in the camps. There had to be preliminary regulations, though I have no doubt at all that from time to time they have been amended and added to as necessity arose.

I want to get it clearly because I want to be absolutely fair to the minister and the ex-minister. Do I take it that these regulations were issued before the camps were laid out, before any difficulties arose, and were sent out to the various camps by the department as being what they considered proper regulations approved by the minister in charge?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
Undoubtedly the
regulations would be sent out before the camps were started at all. I am not prepared1 to say that these precise regulations were sent out from the first, because they would have to be amended from time to time. I am absolutely of the opinion, in spite of what some hon. gentlemen have said, that there is nothing wrong with regulations of that kind. You could not start a camp of that kind and allow an agitator to go in among these young men whose minds are not fully developed and who can be the prey to some agitator in regard to anything-the water, for instance. Some man might have been dismissed for perfectly good reasons and he would be made a martyr of, and
these young men would be gathered together and addressed by some agitator and so trouble would start. To guard against such a possibility some regulations must be put into force. These regulations are merely intended to be helpful; they are not meant to be absolutely lived up to as would a military order in time of war; there is nothing of that kind. But there is in connection with these camps necessity for planning ahead as far as that is possible.
Time is passing and I should like to get into my head exactly what happened with regard to these regulations. The minister makes it clear now that he approves of them.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I say I accept responsibility for them.
The minister said he approved of them; he saw nothing wrong about them. I want to know whether he approved of them before they were sent out.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I do not recall that all were brought to me. Some of them I remember were brought to me and I might mention one in particular. The former Minister of Labour, Mr. Heenan, brought up the question regarding the making of speeches in the camps, and he cited a regulation which forbade people going into camps to make speeches. I looked into the matter and found that there was such a regulation and I changed it, and on the floor of the house I informed him that it had been changed. I had heard of that regulation and thought that it would probably be better to have it changed.

Would anyone else than the minister in charge of that department have authority to send out to all relief camps in Canada such regulations? Would anyone else have authority to send out such regulations without consulting the minister and having his approval?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Whatever was done the minister is responsible for; the hon. gentleman knows very well that it is so. You cannot trace back to find out what an office boy in the department might have done; it is the minister you have to deal with.
This was not an office boy.
Is Brigadier General Spry an office boy?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
I am citing an instance; I am not dealing with that particular case. The ex-Minister of Public Works (Mr. Elliott) wants to trace back somewhere in the
Supply-Defence-Relief Camps

department to the man who wrote a particular letter, and I hold that that is not necessary at all, because there are responsible ministers in charge of departments, and it is their business to be responsible for everything that goes on in the department. I accept responsibility for anything done while I was there.

I think it is only fair to the committee to make it clear that Brigadier General Spry is not responsible for the regulations. As I understand it, he is the officer commanding the district, and he merely states, "I am sending you regulations that have been forwarded to me." There is no responsibility resting on ihim, so far as I can see. I do not at all agree with the exMinister of National Defence, that he is responsible for what someone under him did without his authority and if he did not know about it. If someone without his authority sent out something that he knew nothing about and did not approve, that is a different matter altogether, and he knows that perfectly well. But he now approves of it, and I take it that he approved of it before it went out. But I want him to be frank with the committee.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
I cannot understand exactly what the hon. member does want. In this particular case he evidently wants to find somebody that wrote a letter and to blame him. In most cases-and I have very often heard of this being done-he would only be looking for an opporunity to blame the minister for what happened in his department. That is the general rule. A minister, if something goes wrong in his department, is undoubtedly to blame. I want to go further than this and to say that I cannot see anything particularly out of the way in having among the regulations one of that kind, because it is impossible to run such a camp if you have some organization meeting there and saying: We will go up and complain about something to-day and about something else to-morrow and so on. That would be an impossible situation and make the whole camp and system a prey to agitators. I appeal to the good sense of the committee that the only proper method on which to run such a camp is to impose regulations of that kind. The proof of what I say is that all through eastern Canada and west as far as Calgary the same system has been in force without any trouble arising. It is not only the Department of National Defence that has had these camps run in the same general way, but the Department of the Interior has had similar camps. I must be frank; I do not want to say that the same regulations are in force 
there because I do not know, but the same rate of wages and the same general system of supplies have been in force. I cannot see that there is anything out of the way in what has been the subject of discussion tonight.

I want to say just a word in answer to the minister. While I have and I believe the house generally has the greatest respect for both the ex-Minister of National Defence and the present minister, I was surprised to hear first of all the present minister defending these regulations and I am surprised to hear the ex-minister continuing to defend them. AfteT hearing them read, and I heard them to-night for the first time, while I 'believe we must have discipline in our relief camps as well as in other places-

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: The hon. gentleman does not know the situation or the background involved; I do not think he has a very clear idea of the situation.

One does not need to know the situation to realize that regulations such as have been read here to-night and are contained in that document are surely not proper, decent regulations to send out to govern the conduct of men in these relief camps. That is my very strong impression, and I believe it is the impression of every member of this committee. My knowledge of relief camps is not very extensive, but I know something about them, and while I understand there must be discipline, I believe the men should have a right to submit a grievance, if they have one, to some authority and not be gagged.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: They are not gagged; they have a right to submit their complaints.

I should like to know, if I may, just when these regulations were issued. I should like to see the first order that was sent out instructing that regulations of this kind should be sent out to all the camps. I suggest to the present minister, the ex-minister and all other ministers that these regulations should be revised to the extent of cutting out completely the clauses that sound to me so very objectionable, starting at number four in the document that we heard read to-night.

If the lawyers
have finished examining the minister and the ex-minister, I am just wondering whether it will be in order for a merely practical man to make some suggestions. I have had a good deal to do with camps both military and otherwise, such as mining, lumbering and all

Supply-Defence-Relief Camps
kinds of camps, and I have visited several of those so-called relief camps. We hear a great deal about this twenty cents a day, and I do not think some hon. gentlemen are treating this matter as fairly as they might. I understand that it costs about $34 a month to bake care of each man in the camps, and I think the sum involved should be referred to as $34 a month and not twenty cents a day. The department should keep that fact before those men, and if they were to do so theTe would be less misunderstanding and less trouble.
I can quite understand that regulations are necessary. I have lived under the king's regulations and orders, and having served in both the Canadian and the British army, I have suffered through those regulations as have many more. But it just occurs to me in regard to this matter of complaints, that nobody can deny a man the right to make a complaint if he finds that something is wrong. After all we are Canadians. I would suggest to the minister that I do not think it is up to the men to run around looking for a foreman to whom to make complaints. When I was in the army my turn sometimes came to 'be orderly officer and I had to go through the dining room and other rooms where the men were and ask them if they had any complaints. If they had found sand in the sugar or stones in the beans or a piece of hoof in Flavelle's corned beef, of course they would tell me. I think if a little diplomacy were exercised and the foreman would walk through the camp at meal hours and say: "Well, boys, any complaints?" and show he is human and working with them, a great deal of this trouble would be avoided. I have a relief camp in my constituency; it is not under the Department of National Defence; it is a federal-provincial camp. I know the foremen there and they never have any trouble with their men because they are human and the impression they create with the men is that of working with, not against them. A little humanity, a little common horse sense, is all that is needed.
We are told that these are not military camps, but all I can say is that from the regulations read it would appear that they are. If they are to be run as military camps, they should be made so in every sense of the word. But I would suggest that the fact be kept before these men and the country generally that they are working for $34 a month and not for twenty cents a day. The government I understand are bringing in a minimum wage bill, and I hope when they do introduce it they will apply it first to their 92582-129
own camps, because I am not very proud of this wage of even $34 a month. We should pay the men a fair wage and demand a fair day's work.

Then
they would be out of work.

No, these men are
human and if they are paid a fair wage they will probably do a fair day's work. I hope the time is not very far distant when this happy condition can be brought about and a few of the suggestions I have made in all sincerity will be passed on to the men in charge of the camps.

Before the discussion
started on this phase of the problem, I desired to ask the minister a question on a different aspect of the matter. The discussion has rather thrown a new light on it. From the larger cities one can understand how it is quite easy for these single unemployed homeless men to get into the camps, but it is a problem in the smaller cities and towns. A large number of young men drift around from place to place looking for work; either they cannot find it or the work does not last long and they are again on the streets. They go from door to door begging for meals and help and thus become a burden to the citizens and to the municipalities; for of course they must be fed. Then in connection with the trains, especially on the main lines, these boys are going back and forth all the time at great danger to themselves and great annoyance to the train crews. The whole situation is very unfortunate. My question is: when the cold weather comes and they cannot travel, how can men who find themselves stranded in the smaller cities or towns get into these unemployment camps?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext: By presenting themselves at the camp.
But they are long distances from the camps. They are a burden on the municipality where they happen to be and it is imposible for them to get to a camp.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
My hon. friend surely
realizes that this is a duty which is incumbent on the provinces. First of all the province receives the information, presumably through the municipality concerned. When the province cannot handle the matter it comes to the dominion government and asks its assistance. Then by agreement under certain methods laid down the dominion government comes in and helps. But it does

Supply-Defence-Relief Camps
not remove from the provinces the responsibility of caring for these people.
Carried.

The unemployed need
something more than grunts from the opposite side of the house; a little help would be in order. The minister has stressed, and it has often been stressed here, that these men can take their complaints to the foremen. I find in these regulations the following:
(b) If any man has a complaint or accusation to bring against a member of the supervisory or administrative staff, such complaint should be laid before the camp foreman, who, if necessary, will transmit it to district headquarters or camp superintendent.
As a matter of fact the attitude towards these men is exhibited in these regulations. They have no rights in the matter. They are in the camp because there seems to be no other place to put them. Along with the hon. members for Vancouver 'Centre (Mr. Mackenzie) and Vancouver North (Mr. Munn) I had an opportunity before coming here of meeting some of these men. They made complaints to us that have been substantiated by the statement of the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland) tonight. Not only did the men make the statement on that occasion, but I had occasion myself to intercede with the authorities in Vancouver to reinstate some of them. The moment a man makes a complaint to the foreman the foreman fires him. He is out on the road before the day is finished.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I do not think the hon. member can back up that statement.
My answer to the minister is that I had already read out of the records to-night before he came in-

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
That is one case,
an allegation by someone in Calgary.
It was from someone who investigated the complaints, involving some thirty men.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
But the hon. gentleman states that it is the usual thing that if anyone complains out he goes, which is lot so.
Mr. MadlNNIS:	That was the statement
made before us. The man was anxious to have his statement investigated as to whether or not it was true, and no investigation has yet been held.
TMr. Stirling.]

Hear,
hear. He asked for one.

Further on the instructions say:
Camp foremen are advised to invariably have another member of the supervisory Staff present as a witness to all proceedings.
Yet while the foreman is advised invariably to have another person present, the man making the complaint is not allowed to have anyone present who may substantiate his statement.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Can my hon. friend
substantiate that statement?

It is here in the regulations. Let me read the regulations signed by D. W. B. Spry, D.O.C. military district 13:
(e) It is the duty of the camp foreman to investigate all complaints and, when receiving complaints for transmission to superior authority, to point out to the parties concerned any irregularity in the means they employ in seeking redress. In hearing complaints or statements, et cetera, camp foremen are advised to invariably have another member of the supervisory staff present as a witness to all proceedings.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext: If I may interrupt, I understood the hon. member to say that the man making the complaint might not have anyone with him. That is the statement I asked Rim to substantiate.

I shall do that. Regulations (a) and Ob) read:
(a)	One of the fundamental and most necessary rules for the administration of unemployment relief camps is to forbid' anything bearing the appearance of combination to obtain redress of alleged grievances. Appeals for redress by means of any document bearing the signature of more than one complainant, or by organized committees combining to make a complaint, are strictly forbidden.
(b)	If any man has a complaint or accusation to bring against a member of the supervisory or administrative staff, such complaint should be laid before the camp foreman, who, if necessary, will transmit it to district headquarters or camp superintendent.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext: But it does not say that no friend may be with him.
But if there is more than one it is a combination.

Oh, oh.

That is what it says, and it means it. Further on it says:
(c) If the camp foreman neglects or refuses to attend to a complaint, the complainant may bring the matter to the notice of the district headquarters or camp superintendent.
How is the man to know-
